summary: A list of the official protocols of the time. This RFC is historic. Replaced by RFC 880.

eli5.summary: An official list of the network rules in use, replaced by an updated list.

questions: what are the official internet protocols
which protocols are required vs recommended

subtitle: An official registry of Internet protocols and their standardization status.

tldr.problem: The early Internet needed a clear, authoritative list of which protocols were required, recommended, optional or experimental, and what issues had been found with each.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 840 provides a catalog of protocols organized by layer (network, host, application) with annotations on status, specifications, known problems, references, dependencies and contact people.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is Historic and was replaced by RFC 880 as protocols evolved and new standards emerged.

facts.label: Core protocols
facts.value: IP, ICMP (required); UDP, TCP, Telnet, FTP, SMTP (recommended)

today: RFC 840 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 880 as the Internet evolved and new protocols were developed and standardized.

sections.title: Overview and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 840 identifies the official protocols of the Internet as of April 1983, drawing primarily from the Internet Protocol Transition Workbook (IPTW) dated March 1982. The RFC serves as a reference guide to the protocol specifications and their standardization status.

The document is organized as an outline with each protocol listed under its layer with five types of information: status (required, recommended, elective, or experimental), specification documents, comments on known issues and differences, references to related documents, dependencies on other protocols, and contact information for questions.
sections.eli5: This RFC is a checklist of network rules. For each rule, it tells you if your computer must follow it, should follow it, can follow it, or should only try it in controlled experiments.

sections.title: Status Levels Explained
sections.content:
Required protocols must be implemented by all Internet hosts. Recommended protocols should be implemented by all hosts but are not mandatory. Elective protocols are optional; hosts may implement them or not. Experimental protocols should only be used by hosts participating in coordinated experiments with the protocol contact person. There is also a status of None for documents that discuss concepts but are not themselves protocols.

The RFC notes that several protocols have undergone revisions since the IPTW, particularly the mail protocols (issued separately as Internet Mail Protocols in November 1982) and some Telnet options found in the older ARPANET Protocol Handbook from 1978.
sections.eli5: Required means everyone must use it. Recommended means you should. Elective means you can choose. Experimental means only try it if you are part of a test.

sections.title: Network and Transport Layer Protocols
sections.content:
At the network level, the RFC lists the Internet Protocol (IP, RFC 791) as required and notes several known issues in the specification, particularly confusion about route options and the pointer mechanism. The Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP, RFC 792) is also required and integral to IP. The RFC emphasizes that implementations of IP that omit ICMP are incomplete.

The host level includes UDP (RFC 768, recommended) for simple datagram transmission, and TCP (RFC 793, recommended) for reliable stream delivery. The RFC documents numerous clarifications needed in TCP, including corrections to the Event Processing section, clarification of the push mechanism, guidance on listening servers, maximum segment size defaults, idle connection behavior, and out-of-order segment handling. It also lists several experimental protocols including the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP), Gateway Gateway Protocol (GGP), Stream Protocol, and Network Voice Protocol.
sections.eli5: IP gets packets from one computer to another (required). ICMP helps with network problems (required). UDP sends quick messages without guarantees (recommended). TCP sends messages that are guaranteed to arrive in order (recommended).

sections.title: Application Layer Protocols
sections.content:
At the application level, the RFC covers numerous protocols. Telnet (RFC 764, recommended) provides remote terminal access, though the RFC notes the SYNCH mechanism needs clarification. FTP (RFC 765, recommended) handles file transfer and is accompanied by detailed guidance on data connection management and stream mode reliability. SMTP (RFC 821, recommended) is the mail protocol, revised since the IPTW, with RFC 822 specifying mail header format.

The RFC also lists utility and diagnostic protocols at the elective level: Trivial FTP (TFTP), Remote Job Entry (RJE), NICNAME (directory lookup), HOSTNAME (host table access), Finger, Echo, Discard, and simple services like Daytime and Quote of the Day. Some protocols like the Time Server Protocol are recommended for basic network services.
sections.eli5: Telnet lets you use a remote computer as if you were there. FTP copies files between computers. SMTP sends email. Other protocols do simpler things like tell you the time or list users.

sections.title: Known Issues and Ongoing Work
sections.content:
The RFC includes detailed comments on several important protocols. TCP documentation needs significant revision for Event Processing, the push mechanism, listening server models, maximum segment size, and idle connection handling. FTP guidance addresses data connection port negotiation, the reuse of data connections between file transfers, and the difference in reliability between stream mode (which closes the connection to indicate end-of-file) and block or compressed modes (which do not).

Many protocols that predate TCP are noted as needing updates for use with it. The RFC also points out that some protocols are based on very old specifications (like Telnet options from 1978) that should be updated and reissued.
sections.eli5: The RFC notes that many protocols have small bugs or unclear parts. Some older protocols were written for different networks and need changes to work with the new Internet.
